Can a squatter really take ownership of a house in Iowa?

Only through adverse possession, and Iowa courts make the claimant prove a long list of facts over at least ten years. The Iowa Court of Appeals has described the doctrine as strictly construed, and it requires a claim to be established by "clear and positive proof" (Olsen v. Hennings, 2012).

Moving into an empty house and staying a few months does not come close. The ten-year period applies to the claim itself. What a short-term occupant creates is a removal problem, which the Code handles through a separate fast court process covered further down.

What must someone prove to win an adverse possession claim in Iowa?

The claimant must show hostile, actual, open, exclusive and continuous possession under a claim of right or color of title for at least ten years. The court in Olsen v. Hennings stated that list, and Iowa State University's Center for Agricultural Law and Taxation repeats it in its case summaries.

ElementPlain meaning in Iowa decisions
HostileContrary to the true legal title. It does not require ill will or bad faith.
Actual and openThe claimant really uses the land in a way an owner would, and anyone could see it.
ExclusiveHeld to the exclusion of the true owner.
ContinuousWithout a break across the full period.
Claim of right or color of titleOnly one of the two is needed. Color of title is something that looks like title but is not.
Ten yearsTied to the ten-year limit for actions to recover real property (Iowa Code 614.1).

The Iowa Code's limitation section sets that ten-year window for recovering real property, and the cases build the adverse possession elements around it. The claimant carries the burden at every step.

What does a successful Iowa claim look like?

Reported Iowa wins often involve a neighbor and a strip of land. One example summarized by the Center for Agricultural Law and Taxation is Summit Veterinary Services v. Tindle, decided by the Iowa Court of Appeals in 2017.

  • A couple bought their home in 1977 and paved a driveway with asphalt.
  • In 1979 the owners of a neighboring clinic built a fence along the south side of the driveway, and the husband helped build and maintain it.
  • The couple treated the land north of the fence as theirs, adding carports in 2002 and 2006.
  • In 2015 a new clinic owner had the property surveyed and sued to quiet title. The couple counterclaimed, and the courts ruled for them.

Two points from that summary help owners. A mistaken belief about ownership did not defeat the claim, because the court saw it as good faith in asserting a right. And a claim of right can be shown by using and improving land as an owner would, without paying rent or acknowledging someone else's title.

How is a boundary dispute different from squatting?

A boundary dispute is about where a line runs between two owners, and Iowa has a separate court procedure for it in chapter 650. An owner of land with lost, destroyed or disputed boundaries may sue in district court in the county where the land lies.

A party may plead that the boundaries were recognized and acquiesced in for ten consecutive years (section 650.6). The court may appoint disinterested licensed surveyors to locate the corners, and the commission's report is due within sixty days of appointment, with twenty days afterward to file exceptions (sections 650.7, 650.11 and 650.12). Neighbors can also fix a line by a signed, acknowledged and recorded written agreement with a plat (section 650.17).

If an old fence or driveway edge is the issue, this chapter is usually the better fit than an eviction case.

How can an Iowa owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

The main tool is forcible entry and detainer, a summary court action under chapter 648. It covers entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth, holdovers after a lease, nonpayment of rent, possession after a foreclosure or execution sale, and possession after a valid tax deed (section 648.1).

  • Notice: three days' written notice to quit before suing on any ground except forcible entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth (section 648.3). It can be served by personal service, by a signed acknowledgment from a resident aged 18 or older, or by posting on the main door plus regular and certified mail.
  • Hearing: no later than 8 days from filing, or 15 if the plaintiff asks or consents to a later date (section 648.5).
  • Judgment: if the defendant is found guilty, the court orders removal, and an execution for removal issues within 3 days (section 648.22).
  • Execution time: an order for removal may be carried out only in the daytime (section 648.20).

Timing matters here. Thirty days of peaceable possession by the defendant, with the plaintiff's knowledge, after the cause of action arises bars the forcible entry proceeding (section 648.18). Chapter 648 also does not stop a separate trespass suit or other ways of testing property rights (section 648.17).

Does Iowa treat staying on property after being told to leave as trespass?

Yes, in many cases. Under section 716.7, trespass includes entering or remaining on property without justification after being told to leave or stay out.

The request can come from the owner, a lessee, a person in lawful possession, their agent or employee, or a peace officer or magistrate. It can be given personally, orally or in writing, or through a valid court order under chapter 236. A printed notice conspicuously posted at the main entrance counts too. The text does not carve out vacant buildings, and the general definition of property covers any building or structure, public or private.

Owners who find an unknown person inside should keep a record of when and how they gave notice. That record helps both a police report and a later court filing.

Do special rules extend the ten years for some claims?

Yes. A person under a legal disability gets extra time to start an action. Under section 614.8, a minor has one year after reaching majority, and a person with mental illness has one year after the disability ends.

Chapter 614 also has older-claim rules that interact with title. Section 614.17A bars an action against a record holder in possession if the claim is more than ten years old and the holder has held the chain of title for over ten years, unless the claimant filed a written statement with the county recorder within ten years of when the claim arose (section 614.17A). A person with an unbroken record chain for forty years or more has marketable record title (section 614.31).

These rules are technical. A title examiner or attorney can tell you how they affect a specific parcel.

What should owners of vacant Iowa houses do, and can they still sell?

Start by documenting the property and sending written notice, then use the chapter 648 process if someone remains. Keep dates, photographs and copies of everything you serve.

Occupancy issues do not prevent a sale, but they affect the price and the timing. A title search can turn up recorded claims, and a buyer who plans to close fast has to decide how much risk to take on. Cash Home Buyers buys Iowa houses as-is, including ones with occupants or title questions, and we would look at the facts before making any offer. For a legal read on your own situation, an Iowa attorney is the right call.

More questions about Iowa Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Iowa?

At least ten years of continuous possession that meets every element. The period tracks the ten-year limit for actions to recover real property in Iowa Code 614.1.

Does paying property taxes on land help an adverse possession claim?

Courts look at the stated elements and the overall proof, and an attorney can tell you how a court in your county has treated it.

Can I evict a squatter in Iowa without going to court?

The Iowa Code provides a court process, forcible entry and detainer, for removal. Owners should use that route, and a notice to quit comes first on most grounds.

How long is the notice to quit in Iowa?

Three days of written notice, except when the claim is forcible entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth. Mailed notice is complete four days after deposit.

Can an owner lose land to a neighbor through a fence line?

It can happen. Iowa courts have found adverse possession of a strip along a fence line, as in the 2017 Summit Veterinary case, and chapter 650 allows a boundary to be fixed after ten consecutive years of acquiescence.

title: Iowa Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental
content:
Iowa Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

  • Turn the Iowa Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Iowa House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Does Iowa's landlord tenant law cover a house I rent out and want to sell?

Yes, in most cases. The Iowa Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Chapter 562A of the Iowa Code, covers ordinary rental houses, duplexes and apartments, and it applies to agreements entered into, extended or renewed after January 1, 1979.

The act leaves out a short list of arrangements. These include contract purchasers, employees housed as a condition of the job, hotel and motel stays, owners of condominiums and co-ops, farm rentals, and some nonprofit transitional housing. Mobile home communities fall under a separate chapter, 562B. If your tenant fits one of those exclusions, the rules below may not match your situation, so read the statute or talk to an Iowa attorney first.

For the sale itself, the useful definitions are short. A "resident" is an occupant who is at least 18 years old. A "single family residence" has its own street access and shares no heat, hot water or essential facility with another unit. A rental house you own outright usually meets that description. You can read the full chapter on the Iowa Legislature site.

What happens to the lease and the tenant when an Iowa landlord sells?

A lease does not end because the owner sells. Chapter 562A does not give a seller a way to cancel a fixed-term lease on the day of closing, so the buyer normally takes the property with the tenant and the lease in place.

Three parts of the statute matter at closing:

  • Deposit transfer. Under 562A.12, the deposit, less lawful deductions, goes to the new owner, who must notify the tenant, or it is returned to the tenant. A new owner who tells the tenant in writing what the deposit amount is may rely on that figure if the tenant does not object within 20 days.
  • Disclosure duties. Under 562A.13, the duty to disclose the owner's and manager's names and addresses carries over to a successor owner.
  • Release from later liability. Under 562A.16, a seller who sells in good faith to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for later events once the tenant receives written notice of the sale.

In practice, send the tenant a dated written notice with the buyer's name and the address for rent and repair requests.

Which Iowa notice periods and dollar limits should a landlord keep in mind?

The table below pulls the main numbers from Chapter 562A in one place. The statute controls if anything here conflicts with it.

TopicRuleSection
Security deposit capTwo months' rent562A.12
Deposit return30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives a mailing address562A.12
Rent increaseWritten notice at least 30 days before it takes effect, and not before the term or renewal ends562A.13
Landlord entry24 hours' notice at reasonable times, except emergencies562A.19
Late fee cap, rent up to $700$12 a day or $60 a month562A.9
Late fee cap, rent over $700$20 a day or $100 a month562A.9
Nonpayment of rentThree days after written notice to pay562A.27
Other material breachSeven days to cure after written notice562A.27
Month-to-month ending30 days before the periodic rental date562A.34
Week-to-week ending10 days562A.34

How do Iowa security deposit rules work when a house is sold or the tenant leaves?

An Iowa landlord must either return the deposit or send an itemized written statement within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant provides a mailing address. A landlord who misses that deadline loses the right to withhold anything.

The rest of the deposit rules are just as specific:

  • The deposit must sit in an insured institution and may not be mixed with the landlord's own money.
  • Interest earned in the first five years belongs to the landlord.
  • The landlord carries the burden of proving that a deduction was justified.
  • Bad-faith retention can bring punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, plus actual damages.
  • If the tenant never supplies an address within one year, the deposit reverts to the landlord.

Before you list or sell a rental, find the deposit records and reconcile them. A buyer or title company will ask where the money is, and a gap on this point can slow a closing.

Can a tenant stop me from showing an Iowa rental to buyers?

A tenant may not unreasonably refuse access for showings to purchasers, and a landlord may enter after giving at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times. In an emergency, no notice is needed.

The same section limits landlords. Entering when the law does not allow it, entering at unreasonable times, or using repeated entry demands to harass a tenant lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease. Damages in that situation are at least one month's rent, plus fees (562A.35). A landlord who plans several showings should therefore write down dates and give each notice early.

A tenant who refuses lawful access can face an injunction or lease termination, along with damages and fees.

What repairs must an Iowa landlord make, and what can a tenant do if they are not made?

Iowa landlords must follow the housing codes that affect health and safety, keep the unit fit and habitable, and keep supplied facilities working. That includes plumbing, electrical systems, heating, running water and reasonable hot water, plus clean common areas and waste receptacles (562A.15).

If a landlord falls short, tenants have several routes under the act:

  • Written notice of a material breach, followed by termination if the problem is not fixed within seven days (562A.21).
  • Buying substitute service and deducting the cost, if the landlord cuts heat, water or other essentials on purpose or through neglect (562A.23).
  • Leaving and ending the lease within 14 days after fire or other casualty that substantially impairs use, or paying reduced rent if part of the unit is usable (562A.25).
  • Deducting repair costs, up to one month's rent, when defending a nonpayment claim, if the tenant gave seven days' notice before the rent was due (562A.27).

A seller of a rental house with open repair complaints should expect a buyer to ask about them. Unresolved code issues also raise the retaliation risk described next.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Iowa houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What is landlord retaliation, and what are the self-help limits in Iowa?

Iowa bars a landlord from raising rent, cutting services or filing for possession because a tenant complained to a code agency, complained about a 562A.15 problem, or joined a tenants' union. A good-faith complaint made within the prior year creates a presumption of retaliation (562A.36).

Landlords also may not remove a tenant by their own action. Utility shutoffs, changing locks and similar steps are barred except for abandonment, surrender or what the chapter allows (562A.33). A tenant who is locked out or cut off may recover possession or end the lease, and can seek actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, and attorney fees (562A.26).

Timing a sale to push out a tenant who recently complained is the kind of move this section is written for. If you plan to sell and the tenant has complained in the past year, get advice before you send any notice.

How does an Iowa eviction case move through court?

An Iowa eviction starts with a written notice, then a court filing under Chapter 648, and ends with removal by an officer only after a judgment. The usual first step for unpaid rent is a three-day written notice to quit.

Once a case is filed, Iowa Code 648.5 sets the pace:

  • The court sets a hearing no later than eight days after filing, or up to 15 days if the plaintiff asks or agrees.
  • The tenant must be served at least three days before the hearing, by a signed acknowledgment from a resident aged 18 or older, personal service, or posting plus mailing after two failed attempts.
  • If judgment goes to the landlord, an execution for removal issues within three days, and removal happens in daytime only (648.20 and 648.22).
  • Thirty days of peaceable possession with the landlord's knowledge after the cause of action arose bars the proceeding (648.18).

Notices have their own service rules. They may be served by signed acknowledgment, by personal service, or by posting on the main entrance door plus regular and certified mail, and mailed notice is complete four days after deposit (562A.8 and 562A.29A).

How do Iowa tenant rules affect a quick as-is sale of a rental?

Tenant rights add steps to a sale, but they do not block one. The tenant keeps the lease, the deposit follows the property, and written notice protects the seller from later claims.

A buyer purchasing for cash still inherits the tenancy if the house is occupied, so a clean file helps. Gather these items before you request an offer:

  • The signed lease and any renewals.
  • Deposit amount and where it is held.
  • Dates of repairs, code complaints and entry notices.
  • A draft written notice of the sale for the tenant.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

More questions about Iowa Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

Can an Iowa landlord end a lease just because the house is being sold?

No. Chapter 562A gives no special right to end a lease because of a sale, so a tenant with a fixed term generally stays until it ends. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by either side with written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date.

How much notice must an Iowa landlord give before showing the house?

At least 24 hours, and the visit must happen at reasonable times. Emergencies are the exception. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for showings to purchasers.

Who gets the security deposit when an Iowa rental is sold?

The deposit, less lawful deductions, goes to the new owner, who must tell the tenant, or it is returned to the tenant. The buyer then takes on the deposit duties. The seller should document the amount in writing.

How long does an Iowa landlord have to return a deposit?

Thirty days after the tenancy ends and the landlord receives the tenant's mailing address. The landlord must either return the money or send an itemized written statement of reasons for withholding.

Can I sell an Iowa rental house that has a tenant in it?

Yes. The tenant keeps the lease and the rights under it, and the buyer steps into the landlord role. Give the tenant written notice of the sale, transfer the deposit properly and keep records of repairs and notices.

Iowa Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Iowa Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Iowa Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Iowa House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Iowa?
We buy Iowa houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What eviction notices does Iowa law require from a landlord?

Iowa uses a short written notice first, and the length depends on the reason. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets a three-day notice for unpaid rent, a seven-day notice for most lease violations, and longer notices to end a tenancy without cause.

SituationNoticeStatute
Unpaid rent3 days after written notice562A.27(2)
Lease violation that can be fixedTermination not less than 7 days after receipt562A.27(1)
Same violation again within 6 months7 days written notice, no fix period562A.27(1)
Week-to-week tenancy10 days before the end date562A.34
Month-to-month tenancy30 days before the rental date562A.34

The text of both sections is on the Iowa Legislature site. For unpaid rent, the notice must also state that the landlord intends to terminate.

How does the Iowa three-day nonpayment notice work?

The tenant has three days after the written notice to pay the rent in full, or the landlord may terminate. Section 562A.27(2) ties the notice to rent that is unpaid when due and to the landlord's stated intent to end the lease.

There is one defense worth knowing. A tenant can fight a nonpayment case by proving all of the following:

  • The landlord failed to meet the rental agreement or the repair duty in section 562A.15.
  • The tenant told the landlord at least seven days before the rent due date that they planned to fix the problem at the landlord's cost.
  • The repair cost no more than one month's rent.
  • The tenant made the repair in good faith before receiving the termination notice.

When that defense works, the repair cost is deducted from the rent claimed.

What is the difference between a notice to terminate and a notice to quit?

The termination notice ends the lease, and the notice to quit is the last warning before court. Chapter 648 requires a three-day written notice to quit before a landlord files a forcible entry and detainer case, which is Iowa's name for an eviction lawsuit.

A landlord who already served the three-day nonpayment notice and terminated under 562A.27(2) can file without a second three-day notice to quit, according to Iowa Code chapter 648.

The notice can be delivered by a signed acknowledgment from an adult resident, by personal service, or by posting on the main entrance plus regular and certified mail. Mailed notice is complete four days after it is deposited, whether or not anyone signs for it. Service that does not follow these methods can leave the landlord without a valid notice.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Iowa house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How fast does an Iowa eviction case move?

Quickly. After the landlord files, the court sets the hearing no later than eight days out, or up to fifteen days if the landlord requests or agrees to a later date.

Key timing rules in section 648.5:

  • The tenant must be served at least three days before the hearing.
  • If the hearing is set fewer than three days after service, the tenant must be told of the right to a continuance and gets one on request.
  • No default judgment can be entered without proper service.
  • If a genuine fact dispute exists, the court holds an evidentiary hearing and continues the case.

A tenant who does not show up can lose by default, which orders removal without a hearing on the merits, as the People's Law Iowa guide explains. Tenants may file a written answer before trial, but it is optional, and they can raise defenses and counterclaims at the hearing.

What happens after a landlord wins an Iowa eviction judgment?

The court enters judgment putting the landlord in possession. If the tenant has not left within three days of the judgment, an execution for removal issues.

The landlord then asks the clerk for a writ of possession and schedules the date with the county sheriff. The Johnson County sheriff's page says the office serves the writ, oversees the removal and returns the writ to the court, and that removals must happen in daylight under section 648.20.

The loser has 20 days from judgment to appeal, but a tenant who lost must still move out while the appeal is pending. For a manufactured home in a community, either side can elect within three days to leave the home in place for up to 60 days, with utilities disconnected and no overnight occupancy between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m.

Can a landlord sue a tenant who stays after a lease ends?

Yes. Under 562A.34, a tenant who remains without the landlord's consent after the term can be sued for possession. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord can also recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees.

For repeated rent or lease problems, section 562A.27(3) lets the landlord seek damages and an injunction, and attorney fees if the breach was willful. The tenant is excused only by showing due diligence and circumstances beyond their control.

One more limit: a landlord who knowingly lets the tenant stay peaceably for 30 days after the cause of action arises can be barred from the eviction proceeding under section 648.18. Delay can cost a landlord the case.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Iowa houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Where can Iowa landlords and tenants get help with an eviction?

Iowa Legal Aid runs six eviction help desks across the state, according to People's Law Iowa. Tenants who are served with a hearing notice can start there.

County sheriffs carry out the final step but cannot give legal advice. The Johnson County sheriff recommends serving notices personally and having an attorney draft them, since requirements vary by the reason for the notice. The same page lists a 14-day notice for mobile home tenancies, which is a separate track from the notices in the table above.

Landlords should also call the sheriff ahead of the removal date if pets, vehicles, appliances, firearms or other dangerous items are likely to be inside. Planning for those items avoids delays on the day of the writ.

How does a pending eviction affect selling an Iowa rental house?

It adds time, cost and uncertainty to a listing. A buyer using a lender usually wants a vacant, clean house, and an open court case or an occupied unit is hard to show.

Owners in this spot often weigh a few options:

  • Finish the notice and court steps, then sell the vacant house.
  • Sell with the tenant in place and let the buyer handle the lease.
  • Negotiate a move-out date with the tenant and sell after.

We buy Iowa houses with tenants or damage, and we can talk through which route fits your dates. Whichever you pick, keep copies of every notice, the proof of delivery and any court papers, because the title company and the buyer will ask for them.

Our Iowa landlord tenant guide covers deposits and the rest of the lease rules.

More questions about Iowa Eviction Notice Rules

How many days does a landlord have to give for an eviction in Iowa?

It depends on the reason. Unpaid rent needs a three-day notice, a fixable lease violation needs a seven-day notice, and ending a month-to-month tenancy without cause needs 30 days.

Can an Iowa landlord evict without going to court?

No. After the notice period, the landlord must file a forcible entry and detainer action, win a judgment and have the sheriff carry out the writ. Removals happen only in daylight.

How long do tenants have to leave after a judgment in Iowa?

Three days. If the tenant has not left within three days of the judgment, an execution for removal issues. The loser has 20 days to appeal, but must still move out.

Is there a notice for week-to-week tenants in Iowa?

Yes. Either side can end a week-to-week tenancy with written notice given at least ten days before the termination date.

What if a tenant repeats the same lease violation?

If substantially the same act or omission recurs within six months, the landlord may terminate on at least seven days' written notice, without a new chance to fix it.

Can I sell my Iowa house while the tenant is being evicted?

Yes, an owner can sell at any stage, but the open case and the occupant make a traditional sale harder. A direct sale to a cash buyer avoids showings and repairs.

How does an Iowa tax sale work?

Iowa counties sell delinquent property taxes at an annual public sale, and the buyer receives a certificate, not a deed. On the third Monday in June, the county treasurer offers all parcels with delinquent taxes for sale, although the treasurer may pick a different June date for good cause (Iowa Code 446.7).

The deed comes much later, and only if the owner and other interested parties do not redeem in time. That gap is what gives a homeowner room to act, and it is the reason a lien-style purchase is not the same as owning the house.

Parcels held by a county or city, or owned by the state or a political subdivision, cannot be sold, and a sale of them is void.

What leads up to the June sale?

Taxes first become late, then the owner gets notices, then the parcel is listed. The statewide treasurers' calendar shows the sequence.

WhenWhat happens
September 1First-half installment due, payable through September 30
OctoberUnpaid first half becomes delinquent and begins to accrue interest
March 1Second-half installment due, payable through March 31
AprilUnpaid second half becomes delinquent
By May 1Owner notice of the coming sale mailed first class (section 446.9)
One to three weeks before saleNotice published in an official county newspaper (section 446.9)
Third Monday in JuneAnnual tax sale

Late interest on delinquent installments is 1.5 percent per month, according to the Iowa treasurers' important dates page. A mortgagee or other interested party can ask for its own notice by filing a request one month before the sale with a $25 fee per parcel, valid five years.

Who can bid, and what does the winner get?

Bidders compete on percentage, and the lowest percentage wins. Bids must be at least one percent, and ties are settled by random selection (section 446.16). Bidders need a federal tax identification number and either a registered agent or a verified statement on file, and the treasurer may charge a reasonable registration fee.

If no one bids, or the bid falls below the total due, the county bids the total amount due, and no cash changes hands (section 446.19). Parcels left unsold for want of bidders can be offered again, and a county holding such a public bidder certificate may accept redemption any time before the deed issues.

The certificate holder pays later-year taxes and adds them to the amount the owner must redeem. The holder owns a claim to the parcel, not the parcel.

How much does it cost to redeem an Iowa tax sale parcel?

Redemption costs the sale amount, the certificate fee and later-year amounts, plus interest of 2 percent per month, with each fraction of a month counted as a full month (section 447.1). Interest has a $1 minimum, and payment must reach the treasurer by the last day of the month to avoid another month of interest.

  • Costs of serving the redemption notice, certified mail, any publication and the record search are added to the amount (section 447.13).
  • If the holder is not a county, the record search must be done by an Iowa title guaranty abstractor or an Iowa-licensed attorney, and the search charge is capped at $300.
  • Costs must be filed with the treasurer before redemption is complete, or the treasurer cannot collect them.

Since interest runs from the sale, a delay of even a few weeks can add another full month. A local treasurer can quote the exact payoff; for example, the Linn County Treasurer says its office processes redemptions and tells callers to phone 319-892-5500 for the fee and documents.

How long does an owner have before the right to redeem ends?

The right to redeem lasts at least until ninety days after the redemption notice is completely served. A certificate holder may serve that notice one year and nine months after the sale (section 447.9).

Type of saleEarliest redemption notice
Regular annual saleOne year and nine months after sale
Public bidder sale (446.18)Nine months after sale
Abandoned residential or vacant lot (446.19A) and public nuisance (446.19B) salesThree months after sale

The notice goes by regular and certified mail to the owner and the occupant, and to mortgagees and other record interest holders. If service cannot be made that way, the holder publishes it once in an official county newspaper. Service is complete only when an affidavit is filed with the treasurer, and the right of redemption then runs ninety days (section 447.12).

The deadline is close of business on day 90, or the next business day if day 90 is a weekend or holiday. A postmark does not count, so the payment itself must be received.

Are there protections for owners who cannot pay?

A few narrow ones exist. A county board of supervisors can redeem an owner-occupied residential parcel for an owner who is unable to contribute to public revenue, on petition (section 447.9(3)). A legal representative can redeem for a person with a legal disability before the deed is delivered, and after delivery that person has to bring an equitable action within one year after the disability is removed (section 447.7).

Notice also protects owners. If an owner of record was not served the redemption notice under section 447.9, the tax deed is void, subject to the affidavit rules in sections 448.15 and 448.16 (section 448.3).

These routes are limited. They do not replace paying the taxes or selling the home while the redemption right is still open.

What does an Iowa tax deed do?

The county treasurer issues the deed after the ninety-day period, and the deed vests the state's, the county's and the former owner's interest in the purchaser (sections 448.1 and 448.3). The treasurer records the deed before handing it over and receives $25 per deed.

A deed can be attacked only through an equitable action in district court, and the challenger must prove one of four things: the parcel was not subject to tax, the taxes were paid before the sale, the parcel was redeemed, or there was an entire omission in listing, assessment, levy, notice or sale (section 448.6). Such actions must be brought within three years after the deed is executed and recorded (section 448.12).

A deed holder in possession may also file an affidavit with the county recorder. Other claimants then have 120 days to file a claim and 60 more days to sue, and if no claim is filed, the title is conclusively established (sections 448.15 and 448.16).

Someone who remains in possession after a valid tax deed is subject to forcible entry and detainer (section 648.1).

Can I sell my Iowa house before the tax deed issues?

Yes, in most cases, because the owner keeps title until a deed is delivered. A sale that pays the redemption amount at closing ends the tax sale and clears that debt from the title.

Three practical steps help. Ask the county treasurer for a current redemption figure and the date interest next rolls over. Find out whether a redemption notice has been served, since that sets the ninety-day clock. And line up a buyer who can close before that clock runs out. Cash Home Buyers buys Iowa houses as-is and can move on a short timeline when the facts allow it, and we make no promise on price before reviewing the property.

More questions about Iowa Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales

When is the Iowa tax sale held?

The third Monday in June, unless the county treasurer sets a different June date for good cause.

What interest rate applies to Iowa tax sale redemption?

Two percent per month, and any fraction of a month counts as a full month. Costs and later-year taxes are added.

How long do I have to redeem after the redemption notice?

Ninety days after service of the notice is complete. Payment must be received by close of business on day 90 or the next business day, and a postmark does not count.

Who issues an Iowa tax deed?

The county treasurer, after the ninety-day period, once the purchaser returns the certificate and pays the deed and recording fees.

Can a tax deed be challenged in Iowa?

Yes, but only in an equitable action in district court on narrow grounds, brought within three years of the deed being executed and recorded.

Does Iowa have a tax lien sale or a tax deed sale?

Iowa sells certificates of purchase at the annual sale, and a deed follows only if the property is not redeemed. The buyer's certificate works like a lien until then.
